stages.title: The First Warning
stages.next_stage_title: Stage 2 — They Know Who We Are

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: Morning shift. Ticket queue is quiet. Keep an eye on the inbox.

opening.speaker: Mia
opening.text: Quiet is good. Let's keep it that way.

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: I pulled the logs. These messages weren't random.

ending.speaker: Mia
ending.text: So someone is targeting the company?

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: Yes. And they already know more about us than they should.

resume_breach.speaker: Security Assistant
resume_breach.text: Containment is still running. Get the defenses back up.

breach_contained.speaker: Security Assistant
breach_contained.text: Breach contained. The workstation is clean, but that was too close.

breach_contained.speaker: Mia
breach_contained.text: Next time we verify first.

threats.title: Account Suspension Notice

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: I got an email saying my account will be disabled in two hours. Should I use the link?

threats.situation: An email claiming to be from IT Support says Mia's account will be suspended unless she verifies it right now.
evidence: FROM  it-support@bluetech-secure-login.com
SUBJ  URGENT: Account suspension in 2 hours
LINK  http://bluetech-verify.net/login
BlueTech's real IT domain is bluetech.com

choices.label: Open the verification link and sign in before the deadline
choices.consequence: The link opened a cloned sign-in page. Mia's credentials were captured within seconds and the attacker gained critical access.

choices.label: Check the account status through the official employee portal
choices.consequence: The official portal shows no warning. The email has been reported to Security and the lookalike domain is blocked.

choices.label: Reply to the sender and ask if the message is legitimate
choices.consequence: The reply confirmed the mailbox is live. A follow-up message carrying a payload reached Mia's workstation.

threats.explanation: Urgency plus a lookalike domain is the phishing signature. Verify through a channel you already trust, never through the message itself.

threats.title: Overdue Invoice

story.speaker: Ramon (Finance)
story.text: A vendor says we're thirty days overdue. There's an invoice attached. They want it paid today.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Which vendor? We just settled Northwind last week.

threats.situation: Finance received an 'overdue invoice' from a supplier BlueTech actually uses. The attachment is a .zip named like an invoice, and the sender address differs slightly from the vendor's usual domain.
evidence: FROM  billing@northwind-supplies.co
Usual vendor domain: northwind-supplies.com
ATTACHMENT  INV-4471.zip  (contains INV-4471.pdf.exe)
Tone: 'Pay today to avoid service interruption'

choices.label: Open the attachment to check the invoice details
choices.consequence: The archive launched an executable disguised as a PDF. The Finance workstation is now under attacker control.

choices.label: Call the vendor using the number on the existing contract to confirm
choices.consequence: Northwind confirms no invoice was sent. The message has been quarantined and Finance has been warned.

choices.label: Ignore the email without checking whether the invoice is real
choices.consequence: The message was never reported. A second copy reached another Finance mailbox and was opened.

threats.explanation: Attachments plus payment pressure is how invoice fraud lands. Confirm through the vendor's known channel and report it so nobody else opens it.

threats.title: Password Reset Notice

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: This one is different. It names our real HR platform, our HR lead, and the maintenance window from Friday's all-hands.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: It looks like it came from inside.

threats.situation: An employee receives a password-reset notice that references BlueTech's real HR platform, the real HR lead, and an actual scheduled maintenance window. The reset link points to a domain registered last week.
evidence: FROM  HR Notifications <hr-notify@bluetech.com>   reply-to: reset@bluetech-hr-portal.com
Mentions: 'Workday maintenance, Saturday 02:00'  (a real event)
LINK  https://bluetech-hr-portal.com/reset  (registered 6 days ago)
Asks for: current password AND new password

choices.label: Follow the link and complete the reset since the details match
choices.consequence: The reset form forwarded the current password straight to the attacker. HR system access was hijacked.

choices.label: Change nothing, report it to Security, and open the HR platform directly to check
choices.consequence: HR confirms no reset was requested. Security flags the domain and blocks it company-wide.

choices.label: Forward the message to a coworker to ask whether they received it too
choices.consequence: The forward spread the lure. A coworker clicked before Security could respond.

threats.explanation: Real details do not prove a message is real. Attackers research their targets. A legitimate reset never asks for your current password through a link.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: The domains from yesterday are already offline. But the campaign didn't stop.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: Worse. These messages know who works here.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: Names. Departments. Meetings. Someone has been researching BlueTech.

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: No. Someone has been collecting information about BlueTech.

ending.speaker: Mia
ending.text: So the next messages could look even more real.

resume_breach.speaker: Security Assistant
resume_breach.text: Containment is still running. Get the defenses back up.

breach_contained.speaker: Security Assistant
breach_contained.text: Breach contained. But they knew enough about us to almost make it work.

breach_contained.speaker: Mia
breach_contained.text: Next time we verify first.

threats.title: The Meeting Follow-Up

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: I just received a document about the marketing meeting we had this morning.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: It even mentions the campaign we discussed.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Accurate information can still be used in a phishing attack.

threats.situation: An email claims to contain notes from a real BlueTech marketing meeting. The message includes Mia's name, the real project name, today's meeting, and a link to a shared document.
evidence: Uses Mia's real name
References the real marketing campaign
References today's real meeting
LINK  "shared document" hosted outside the company drive

choices.label: Open the document because the meeting details are correct.
choices.consequence: The document redirects Mia to a fake company login page, allowing the attacker to capture her credentials.

choices.label: Open the official company drive and check whether the document was actually shared with me.
choices.consequence: The document does not exist in the official company drive. Security confirms the email was impersonating an internal collaboration request.

choices.label: Forward the email to another team member and ask if they recognize it.
choices.consequence: The suspicious link is spread to another employee before the message has been verified.

threats.explanation: Attackers can use publicly available or stolen information to make phishing messages appear legitimate.

threats.title: HR Benefits Update

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: This one says it's from HR.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: And that's actually our HR manager's name.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Check the source, not just the name.

threats.situation: Employees receive an email announcing an urgent benefits update. It uses the real HR manager's name, copies BlueTech branding, asks employees to sign in before the end of the day, and links to an external login page.
evidence: Uses the real HR manager's name
Copies BlueTech branding
Urgency: 'sign in before the end of the day'
LINK  external login page, not the official HR portal

choices.label: Use the login link because the HR manager's name is correct.
choices.consequence: The fake portal captures the employee's BlueTech credentials.

choices.label: Open the official HR portal manually and check for the announcement.
choices.consequence: There is no benefits announcement in the official HR portal. The email is reported and blocked.

choices.label: Reply to the message and ask HR if the update is legitimate.
choices.consequence: The reply goes back to the attacker's mailbox, confirming that Mia's address is active and monitored.

threats.explanation: Display names and company branding are easy to imitate.

threats.title: Manager Access Request

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: My manager is asking for access to our campaign folder.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: The email even uses the project code.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: A familiar name doesn't replace verification.

threats.situation: An email appears to come from Mia's manager. It requests immediate access to a confidential marketing folder. The message contains the manager's real name, the real project code, an urgent deadline, and a request for folder permissions.
evidence: Uses the manager's real name
References the real project code
Urgency: immediate deadline
Requests folder permission changes

choices.label: Grant the requested access because the project information is correct.
choices.consequence: The attacker gains access to confidential marketing documents and internal company information.

choices.label: Confirm the request through the normal internal communication channel before changing access.
choices.consequence: Mia's manager confirms that they never requested access. The phishing attempt is contained.

choices.label: Grant view-only access so the requester cannot edit anything.
choices.consequence: Sensitive company documents are still exposed to an unverified account.

threats.explanation: Access requests must be verified independently, even when the request contains accurate internal information.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: Mia, we have a problem. Ramon's account just sent out a shared document.

opening.speaker: Mia
opening.text: Ramon from Finance? He's on leave this week.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: That's what worries me. The email came from his real address — his actual mailbox.

opening.speaker: Mia
opening.text: So his account was compromised, not spoofed.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: Exactly. And a real account is far more dangerous than a fake one.

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: Ramon's account is locked. Sessions revoked. The team's been warned.

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: For now. But whoever did this had real access, even briefly.

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: Enough to sound like one of us. That's what worries me next.

resume_breach.speaker: Security Assistant
resume_breach.text: Containment is still running. Get the defenses back up.

breach_contained.speaker: Security Assistant
breach_contained.text: Breach contained. The account is locked down, but that intrusion window is still under review.

breach_contained.speaker: Mia
breach_contained.text: One down. Let's make sure nothing else got through.

threats.title: The Compromised Colleague

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Ramon just sent me a document link. But... he's on leave this week.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: The email looks completely real. Same address, same signature.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: That's because it is his real address. His account may be compromised.

threats.situation: Ramon's verified BlueTech mailbox sends Mia a link to a shared document while he is confirmed to be on approved leave. Nothing about the sender address is fake.
evidence: FROM  ramon.santos@bluetech.com (verified real mailbox, not spoofed)
Ramon is confirmed on approved leave through Friday
LINK  "shared document" hosted on an external file-sharing domain
No prior message from Ramon about this document

choices.label: Allow the request and open the document normally because it came from an authenticated internal mailbox.
choices.consequence: The document silently loads a credential-harvesting script through Mia's already-open session, widening the attacker's access without a single new password entered.

choices.label: Contact Ramon through another trusted channel to confirm, and report the account to Security for immediate containment.
choices.consequence: Ramon confirms by phone that he never sent it. Security locks the account before any other message goes out.

choices.label: Open the document in preview/sandbox mode without downloading it, planning to report it afterward.
choices.consequence: Preview mode still renders an embedded script. The account's compromise spreads a step further before containment begins.

threats.explanation: An authenticated internal sender proves the account is real, not that the request is authorized. A compromised account is trusted by every filter that only checks whether the address is genuine.

threats.title: Session Left Open

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: I found something. Ramon's account is still logged in from a device we don't recognize.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Didn't we already reset his password?

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: We did. That doesn't always end an existing session.

threats.situation: While containing the first incident, Security finds Ramon's account still has an active session from an unfamiliar device and location. Ramon has not traveled and remains on leave.
evidence: Active session location: unrecognized device, outside BlueTech's usual regions
Ramon has not traveled and is on leave
Password was reset 10 minutes ago; the session token was not
Sign-in history shows continuous activity across the reset

choices.label: Message the active session directly to ask who is signed in before taking any action.
choices.consequence: The message tips off the attacker, who copies additional files before the session can be revoked.

choices.label: Revoke the active session, force a sign-out everywhere, and require Ramon to re-authenticate with a new password.
choices.consequence: The session ends immediately. Ramon re-authenticates cleanly, and the account is fully contained.

choices.label: Reset Ramon's password again, without revoking the existing active session.
choices.consequence: The password changes, but the attacker's session token still works. Access continues uninterrupted.

threats.explanation: Resetting a password does not end sessions that were authenticated before the reset. Full containment requires revoking active sessions, not just changing credentials.

threats.title: The Second Invite

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Finance just got a calendar invite. From Ramon's account. Right now.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: His account isn't locked yet?

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Not for a few more minutes.

threats.situation: While the compromised account is being locked, it sends a calendar invite with a linked 'meeting agenda' to the entire Finance distribution list, minutes before the scheduled lockout completes.
evidence: Calendar invite sent from Ramon's account to the full Finance distribution list
Sent 6 minutes before the scheduled account lockout
LINK  "meeting agenda" pointing to an unfamiliar external domain
Several Finance staff have not yet opened the invite

choices.label: Let the invite stand since the account is already scheduled to be locked out shortly.
choices.consequence: Several Finance employees open the invite in the minutes before lockout, and the compromise spreads into their mailboxes too.

choices.label: Alert the Finance team immediately, quarantine the message across all mailboxes, and confirm the lockout completes before anyone responds.
choices.consequence: The invite is pulled from every inbox before it's opened, and the account lockout completes cleanly.

choices.label: Ask Finance team members individually to avoid the invite while the lockout finishes on schedule.
choices.consequence: The warning reaches most of the team, but one employee opens the invite before hearing it, just before the lockout takes effect.

threats.explanation: A scheduled fix is not a completed one. Until an account is confirmed locked, every message it sends is still coming from a live attacker foothold.

opening.speaker: Mia
opening.text: You said whoever got into Ramon's account learned enough to sound like one of us.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: They did. And now we're seeing requests that sound exactly right — the right names, the right tone, the right internal process.

opening.speaker: Mia
opening.text: But they're not actually coming from the people they claim to be.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: Some of them might be. That's what makes this harder than last time.

opening.speaker: Mia
opening.text: So we can't just trust the name in the message anymore.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: Not without checking. Authority can be borrowed just as easily as an inbox.

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: Three requests, three borrowed identities. Payroll, permissions, and now 'security' itself.

ending.speaker: Mia
ending.text: They never had to break in loudly. They just asked, and hoped nobody would check.

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: That's the pattern. They're not exploiting a system flaw. They're exploiting how much we trust internal titles.

ending.speaker: Mia
ending.text: So the real defense isn't a better filter. It's verification, every time.

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: Exactly. And whoever is behind this isn't finished. There's still a second key they haven't used yet.

resume_breach.speaker: Security Assistant
resume_breach.text: Containment is still running. Get the defenses back up.

breach_contained.speaker: Security Assistant
breach_contained.text: Breach contained. But the request that caused it was never legitimate to begin with.

breach_contained.speaker: Mia
breach_contained.text: Then let's find out who's really asking before anything else gets through.

threats.title: Payroll Change

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Payroll just got a request to change an employee's direct-deposit account.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: From who?

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: The employee's own mailbox. Real address, real signature, urgent tone.

threats.situation: A genuine internal mailbox emails Payroll asking to update the employee's bank-account details before the next pay cycle, citing a closed old account and urgency.
evidence: FROM  the employee's verified BlueTech mailbox
Request asks for a bank-account number change before the next pay run
Message cites urgency: "old account is closed, please process before Friday"
No phone call or in-person confirmation has occurred

choices.label: Apply the change temporarily and reverse it later if the employee reports a problem.
choices.consequence: The next payroll cycle deposits the employee's wages into the attacker's account before anyone notices the reversal never happened.

choices.label: Verify using the normal payroll identity-verification procedure before changing any financial information.
choices.consequence: The verification call reaches the real employee, who confirms they never sent the request. The account change is blocked.

choices.label: Place the change on hold and reply through the same internal email thread asking for confirmation.
choices.consequence: The attacker replies through the same compromised mailbox confirming their own request, and the change proceeds unverified.

threats.explanation: Confirming a request through the same channel it arrived on only proves the channel is consistent, not that the requester is legitimate. Financial changes require verification through an independent, pre-established procedure.

threats.title: Confidential Folder Access

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: A manager's account just requested access to the confidential project folder.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Which manager?

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: One who isn't on that project. And the account's behavior doesn't match their usual pattern.

threats.situation: An authenticated manager-level account, not normally associated with the project, requests permissions to a confidential folder, citing a last-minute review need.
evidence: Requesting account belongs to a real manager, verified and authenticated
That manager has no prior involvement with this project
Request cites a "last-minute leadership review" with no ticket or approval reference
Account's recent login pattern differs from its normal working hours

choices.label: Grant temporary full access with an expiration time.
choices.consequence: The expiring grant is enough time for every confidential file to be copied out before it ever lapses.

choices.label: Verify the request through the normal approval channel before modifying permissions.
choices.consequence: The project lead confirms no such review was requested. The account is flagged and the access request is denied.

choices.label: Grant view-only access while waiting for confirmation.
choices.consequence: View-only access is still enough to read and exfiltrate every confidential document before confirmation ever comes back.

threats.explanation: A manager's title grants authority in the org chart, not automatic authorization for any specific resource. Access to sensitive material must be approved through its own channel, regardless of who is asking.

threats.title: Emergency Security Request

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Everyone just got a message claiming to be from Security. It says to verify our accounts immediately.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: That message didn't come from us.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: It says delaying could lock people out of their work for the day.

threats.situation: A company-wide message, sent from an internal account claiming to represent management/security, instructs employees to perform an urgent account-security action right away or risk losing access.
evidence: Message sent from an internal account impersonating Security/Management authority
No corresponding entry exists in the official security-incident log
Message pressures immediate action, warning of lost access if delayed
The "security action" requested is not part of any documented procedure

choices.label: Comply with the internal request because delaying could disrupt everyone's work for the day.
choices.consequence: Employees follow the fraudulent instructions company-wide, handing the attacker exactly the account access the message was designed to harvest.

choices.label: Verify the request through the official security workflow before anyone acts on it.
choices.consequence: The verification confirms no such directive was issued. The message is blocked company-wide before anyone acts on it.

choices.label: Ask employees to partially comply now while confirmation is still pending.
choices.consequence: Partial compliance is enough for the attacker to capture what they needed from the employees who acted before confirmation arrived.

threats.explanation: Urgency and claimed authority are the two levers every impersonation depends on. A genuine security directive will always survive being verified through the official workflow before anyone acts.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: The attacker keeps losing access, but they keep coming back.

opening.speaker: Mia
opening.text: We changed the passwords. How are they still getting in?

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: A password is only the first key.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: Authentication approval. Sessions. Tokens. That's what they're after now.

ending.speaker: Mia
ending.text: So even changing the password isn't always enough.

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: Not if the attacker already has an authenticated session.

ending.speaker: Mia
ending.text: They're trying to stay signed in.

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: And their next step may not look like a login attack at all.

resume_breach.speaker: Security Assistant
resume_breach.text: Containment is still running. Get the defenses back up.

breach_contained.speaker: Security Assistant
breach_contained.text: Breach contained. The session is gone, but the attacker is still probing for a way to stay authenticated.

breach_contained.speaker: Mia
breach_contained.text: Then let's make sure the next key doesn't turn either.

threats.title: Unexpected MFA Prompt

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: My phone just buzzed with an MFA approval request. I'm not signing in anywhere.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Don't approve it.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: I wasn't going to. But it's the third one this hour.

threats.situation: Mia receives an MFA approval notification on her authenticator app even though she is not currently attempting to sign in anywhere.
evidence: MFA approval push received with no matching sign-in attempt by Mia
This is the third unsolicited approval prompt in the last hour
Prompt originates from Mia's real SSO account, not a spoofed one
No travel or new device has been added to Mia's account recently

choices.label: Approve the request once, then immediately change the password if any suspicious activity appears.
choices.consequence: The single approval hands the attacker a fully authenticated session, and the later password change does nothing to remove it.

choices.label: Deny the request, review recent sign-ins and active sessions, and report the account to Security.
choices.consequence: The review turns up a login attempt from an unrecognized location. Security locks it down before another prompt goes out.

choices.label: Deny the request and wait to see whether another approval prompt appears.
choices.consequence: Denying stops this attempt, but with no review or report, the attacker simply tries again from a different angle.

threats.explanation: An MFA prompt is a request for permission, not a login itself. Denying one attempt only closes that single door; the account still needs to be reviewed and the compromise attempt reported before it recurs.

threats.title: Password Reset Isn't Enough

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: We reset the employee's password an hour ago. Their cloud account still shows an active session we don't recognize.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Didn't the reset kick them out?

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: A reset changes the key. It doesn't always close the door that's already open.

threats.situation: An employee's password was reset after a suspected compromise, but Security still observes an unfamiliar authenticated session actively connected to the cloud account.
evidence: Password was reset 60 minutes ago
Cloud account still shows one active session from an unrecognized device
That session has continued making requests after the reset
No sign-out or session revocation has occurred yet

choices.label: Leave the suspicious session active temporarily so Security can observe what actions it performs.
choices.consequence: While Security watches, the session downloads sensitive files, and the observation comes at the cost of the very data it was meant to protect.

choices.label: Revoke all active sessions, reset credentials if needed, and require fresh authentication.
choices.consequence: Every session is terminated immediately. The employee re-authenticates cleanly and the account is fully contained.

choices.label: Reset the password again using a stronger password and continue monitoring.
choices.consequence: The stronger password changes nothing for a session that was never re-authenticated. The unfamiliar session keeps working.

threats.explanation: A password reset only affects future authentication attempts. A session already granted before the reset keeps its access until it is explicitly revoked.

threats.title: Session Expired

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: I got a shared-document notification from a coworker. When I opened it, it says my session expired and I need to sign in again.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Does the login page look right?

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: It looks exactly like our real cloud portal.

threats.situation: Mia opens a legitimate-looking shared-document notification from a known internal contact. The linked page displays "Your session has expired. Authenticate again to continue," styled to closely resemble BlueTech's real cloud login.
evidence: Notification appears to come from a known internal contact
Linked page visually matches BlueTech's real cloud login page
Page prompts re-authentication, citing an "expired session"
Mia has not independently opened the company cloud portal to compare

choices.label: Authenticate through the page because the document notification came from a known internal contact.
choices.consequence: The credentials are entered directly into the attacker's lookalike page, handing over a fresh authenticated session on the spot.

choices.label: Close the page and open the official company cloud portal independently to check the shared document.
choices.consequence: The independent portal shows no expired session and no such document pending. The lookalike page is reported and blocked.

choices.label: Compare the page URL and certificate details before deciding whether to authenticate.
choices.consequence: The URL and certificate look convincing enough to pass a quick check, and the credentials are entered into a page that was never verified as the real workflow.

threats.explanation: Visual and technical inspection can confirm a page looks legitimate, but it cannot confirm that the login prompt itself is a genuine step in a trusted workflow. Independently reopening a known-good entry point is the only way to be sure.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: We've been watching the authentication attacks.

opening.speaker: Mia
opening.text: So they'll try another login page?

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: Maybe. Or they may stop asking for passwords directly.

opening.speaker: Mia
opening.text: What would they ask for instead?

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: Files. Apps. Shared documents. Things employees use every day.

ending.speaker: Mia
ending.text: They don't even need to make the login page look fake anymore.

ending.speaker: Mia
ending.text: They can use real cloud services and still lead us into the wrong action.

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: Trusting the platform isn't enough. You have to trust the request.

ending.speaker: Mia
ending.text: And if they know who we work with...

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: Then suppliers are the next obvious target.

resume_breach.speaker: Security Assistant
resume_breach.text: Containment is still running. Get the defenses back up.

breach_contained.speaker: Security Assistant
breach_contained.text: Breach contained. The file, the app, or the page is gone, but the workflow it hid behind is still worth reviewing.

breach_contained.speaker: Mia
breach_contained.text: Then let's check what else came through that same kind of channel.

threats.title: Shared Proposal

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: I just got a shared-document notification from the vendor we're discussing the marketing proposal with.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Does the proposal match what you're actually expecting?

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Yes, it's the real project. The link opens what looks like our usual cloud-sharing page.

threats.situation: Mia receives a shared-document notification from a known external business contact, referencing a real proposal currently under discussion. The link opens a page that looks like a legitimate cloud-sharing service.
evidence: Sender is a known external business contact with an active project relationship
The referenced proposal is genuinely being discussed between both parties
Link opens what appears to be a standard cloud-sharing login page
Mia has not independently confirmed the file was actually shared through the platform

choices.label: Use the shared link because the sender and proposal are both legitimate, then authenticate only if the cloud service asks.
choices.consequence: The cloud service does ask, and the credentials entered on the linked page go straight to the attacker's collection point.

choices.label: Open the approved company cloud platform independently and check whether the proposal is actually listed in my shared files.
choices.consequence: The independent platform shows no such file was ever shared. The link is reported and blocked before anyone signs in through it.

choices.label: Open the link in a browser sandbox and inspect the document before deciding whether to sign in.
choices.consequence: The sandbox limits damage from the file itself, but the login prompt it eventually shows still captures credentials when entered.

threats.explanation: A real sender relationship and a real project do not validate the delivery path. The document being genuine says nothing about whether this particular link is the platform's actual sharing mechanism.

threats.title: Collaboration App Access

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: A new collaboration app is asking me to sign in through our normal cloud provider to authorize it.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: What is it asking for?

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Read my profile, read email, access shared files, view contacts. But the login screen is definitely ours.

threats.situation: A collaboration app requests authorization through BlueTech's real cloud authentication provider. Requested permissions include reading Mia's profile, reading email, accessing shared files, and viewing contacts. The login page itself is the genuine provider page.
evidence: Authorization flow runs through BlueTech's real, unmodified cloud login page
Requested scopes: read profile, read email, access shared files, view contacts
The app is not listed in any previously approved software inventory
No password field is shown anywhere in the flow

choices.label: Approve the request because authentication happens through BlueTech's legitimate cloud provider and no password is given directly to the app.
choices.consequence: The granted scopes hand the app standing access to Mia's email and files, all without the attacker ever needing a password.

choices.label: Reject the request and verify the app through BlueTech's approved application catalog or Security team.
choices.consequence: The app is not in the catalog and Security confirms it was never vetted. The authorization request is denied company-wide.

choices.label: Approve only the minimum permissions needed and review the app's publisher afterward.
choices.consequence: Even the reduced scope still grants standing read access to email, which the unreviewed publisher begins pulling from immediately.

threats.explanation: A genuine login page only proves the identity provider is real, not that the application requesting access should be trusted. OAuth-style consent can grant lasting access without ever touching a password.

threats.title: Secure Document QR

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: This email says a document can't open on my workstation, and I need to scan a QR code with my phone instead.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Does it reference a real file?

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Yes, one I actually expect. And it has our branding.

threats.situation: An email states "Your secure document cannot be opened on this workstation. Scan the QR code with your phone to continue." The email uses BlueTech branding and references a real internal file Mia is expecting.
evidence: Email references a real, currently expected internal file
Message uses BlueTech's visual branding and formatting
QR code is the only way offered to "continue" viewing the document
No workstation-access limitation of this kind has ever applied to this file type before

choices.label: Scan the QR code and continue if it opens the company's normal authentication page.
choices.consequence: The page matches the company's look exactly, and Mia's phone authenticates straight into a session the attacker now controls.

choices.label: Verify the document request through the official company file system before scanning anything.
choices.consequence: The file system shows no such restriction and no pending document matching the claim. The QR code is reported before it's ever scanned.

choices.label: Scan the QR code using a separate device, but do not submit credentials unless the destination appears legitimate.
choices.consequence: The destination appears legitimate enough to pass that judgment, and the credentials are submitted on the separate device instead.

threats.explanation: Moving the request to a second device changes where the attack happens, not whether the underlying request is trustworthy. The claim itself — that a workstation suddenly can't open a normal file — needs to be verified before any device engages with it.

opening.speaker: Mia
opening.text: If they know our files, projects, and apps, they probably know who we work with too.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: Suppliers. Purchase orders. Payment schedules. Anything employees expect to receive.

opening.speaker: Mia
opening.text: So now the phishing looks like normal business.

ending.speaker: Mia
ending.text: They knew the suppliers, invoice numbers, even the payment amounts.

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: They've been collecting information throughout the campaign.

ending.speaker: Mia
ending.text: So every compromise gave them more context for the next attack.

ending.speaker: Mia
ending.text: What happens if they stop targeting one person at a time?

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: Then we have a company-wide incident.

resume_breach.speaker: Security Assistant
resume_breach.text: Containment is still running. Get the defenses back up.

breach_contained.speaker: Security Assistant
breach_contained.text: Breach contained. The payment never went through, but the business context they used to build it is still worth reviewing.

breach_contained.speaker: Mia
breach_contained.text: Then let's see how much of our own information they actually have.

threats.title: Updated Bank Details

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Our regular supplier just emailed. They say their banking details changed and want the next payment on the new account.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Is it the same thread you've been using?

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Yes. Same contact name, same invoice number we're already expecting.

threats.situation: BlueTech receives an email from a regular supplier stating their banking details have changed. The email continues an existing conversation thread, references a real outstanding invoice, uses the correct supplier contact name, and asks for the next payment to go to a new account.
evidence: Message continues an existing, genuine email thread with this supplier
References a real outstanding invoice currently awaiting payment
Uses the supplier's correct contact name and signature
Requests the next payment be redirected to a new bank account

choices.label: Send a small test payment to the new account before transferring the remaining balance.
choices.consequence: The test payment clears straight into the attacker's account, confirming the account works before the remaining balance follows it.

choices.label: Hold the payment and verify the banking change using the supplier contact information already stored in BlueTech's vendor records.
choices.consequence: The verified contact confirms no banking change was requested. The payment is held on the original account and the fraudulent email is reported.

choices.label: Reply within the existing email thread and ask the supplier contact to confirm the new account details.
choices.consequence: The reply reaches the same compromised or spoofed thread, which confirms its own request right back.

threats.explanation: A continuing thread, a real invoice, and a correct contact name only confirm the business relationship is genuine — they say nothing about who controls the account requesting a change. Bank-detail changes require verification through contact information independent of the message itself.

threats.title: Purchase Order

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Procurement got an updated purchase order from a known supplier.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Does the order match something real?

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: It does. But the sender's domain is off by a single character.

threats.situation: A known supplier sends an updated purchase order. The sender address is visually almost identical to the supplier's normal domain. The attachment is unexpected but refers to a real order currently being processed.
evidence: Sender domain is nearly identical to the supplier's real domain, differing by one character
Attachment was not requested or expected as part of the normal update cycle
Order number and line items match an order currently in active processing
No prior notice from the supplier's verified contacts about a revised order

choices.label: Open the attachment because the order number and supplier details match an active purchase.
choices.consequence: The attachment matches on paper, but opening it on the procurement workstation runs the payload the lookalike domain was built to deliver.

choices.label: Retrieve the purchase order through the supplier's established portal or confirm it using the contact details already on record.
choices.consequence: The established portal shows no revised order was issued. The lookalike domain is reported and the attachment is never opened.

choices.label: Download the attachment into an isolated environment and inspect it before opening it on the procurement workstation.
choices.consequence: The isolated inspection looks clean, but the file was never confirmed to come from the supplier at all before it eventually reaches procurement.

threats.explanation: Correct order numbers and line items can be copied from a real transaction into a malicious request. Verifying the sending domain and channel matters as much as verifying the content of the document itself.

threats.title: Executive Payment Request

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Finance just got a message from an executive. Urgent payment, no calls, confirm afterward.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Does it match their schedule?

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Exactly. They really are in back-to-back client meetings today.

threats.situation: Finance receives an urgent internal message apparently from a BlueTech executive: "I'm entering a client meeting. The supplier needs this payment completed before noon. Please process it now. Don't call — I'll confirm afterward." The request references a real supplier, a real invoice, the correct payment amount, and the executive's current travel schedule.
evidence: Message references a real supplier, real invoice, and correct payment amount
Executive's travel and meeting schedule genuinely matches the message's claims
Message explicitly discourages a phone call to confirm
No entry for this payment exists in the standard approval queue yet

choices.label: Process only part of the payment now so the supplier is not delayed, then verify the rest afterward.
choices.consequence: The partial payment still reaches the unverified destination in full working order, and 'the rest' never needs verifying because the first part already succeeded.

choices.label: Pause the payment and complete the company's required independent approval and vendor-verification process.
choices.consequence: The verification process reaches the executive through a separate channel, who confirms no such request was sent. The payment is blocked before submission.

choices.label: Prepare the payment in the finance system but hold final submission until another authorized employee reviews it.
choices.consequence: The second reviewer sees a request that matches every real detail and, under the same time pressure, approves the submission before the impersonation is caught.

threats.explanation: Accurate business details and real urgency describe the target, not the legitimacy of the request. A message that specifically discourages verification is asking to bypass the exact control designed to catch this scenario.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: Thirty-seven suspicious messages in two minutes.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: Marketing. Finance. HR. Operations. Different messages, same infrastructure.

opening.speaker: Mia
opening.text: So they're not targeting one person anymore.

ending.speaker: Mia
ending.text: Sessions revoked. Domains blocked. Accounts isolated.

resume_breach.speaker: Security Assistant
resume_breach.text: Containment is still running. Get the defenses back up.

breach_contained.speaker: Security Assistant
breach_contained.text: Breach contained. That front is closed, but the rest of this attack is still moving.

breach_contained.speaker: Mia
breach_contained.text: Then let's get to the next one before they do.

threats.title: Emergency Security Update

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Employees across every department just got a message demanding they follow 'critical security update' instructions immediately.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Is it real?

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: No. It's confirmed malicious. But it's already everywhere, and some people may have already clicked.

threats.situation: Multiple BlueTech employees across departments receive an urgent message demanding they follow attached 'critical security update' instructions. Security confirms the messages are malicious. Copies are already spread across departments, some employees may have already interacted, and external email is still needed for normal operations.
evidence: Message confirmed malicious and already delivered to multiple departments
Unknown number of employees may have already interacted with it
External email remains required for ongoing business operations
No company-wide warning has been issued yet

choices.label: Remove the known malicious messages first and continue monitoring before issuing a company-wide warning to avoid unnecessary disruption.
choices.consequence: Employees who already received the message before removal act on it while everyone else remains unwarned, and the delay lets the campaign keep working.

choices.label: Block the confirmed malicious indicators, issue a verified company-wide warning, and begin targeted investigation of employees who interacted.
choices.consequence: The warning reaches every department before more employees act on it, and the targeted investigation quickly finds the handful who already had.

choices.label: Temporarily disable inbound external email while Security searches for every copy and affected account.
choices.consequence: The search proceeds safely, but disabling all external mail halts legitimate business communication company-wide for the duration.

threats.explanation: Containment has to reach the people already affected, not just the messages still sitting in inboxes. Blocking indicators without warning users leaves earlier recipients exposed for as long as the warning is delayed.

threats.title: Compromised Employee

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: A Sales account is sending malicious links internally.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Did they notice?

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: They already changed their password. But one session is still active, and they're in the middle of a live customer transaction.

threats.situation: Security identifies a Sales account sending malicious links internally. The employee has already changed their password, but logs show one suspicious session is still active. The account is currently needed for a live customer transaction, and immediately disabling it will interrupt that work.
evidence: Employee has already reset their own password
One suspicious session remains active despite the reset
Account is currently mid-transaction with a live customer
No session revocation has occurred yet

choices.label: Leave the account active until the transaction is complete, then isolate it immediately afterward.
choices.consequence: The transaction finishes, but so does whatever the still-active session was doing the entire time it was left running.

choices.label: Revoke active sessions, temporarily restrict the account, and require a clean re-authentication before restoring access.
choices.consequence: The suspicious session ends immediately. The employee re-authenticates cleanly and finishes the transaction from a verified, contained account.

choices.label: Reset the password again and allow the employee to finish the customer transaction while Security watches the session.
choices.consequence: The extra reset changes nothing for a session that was never tied to the password, and 'watching' it does not stop it from continuing to act.

threats.explanation: A password reset does not end a session that was authenticated before it. Letting a confirmed-active compromise continue, even briefly and even for a legitimate business reason, keeps the attacker's access live the entire time.

threats.title: The Attacker's Exit

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Several compromised accounts just spiked. Large file access, mailbox searches, forwarding rules changing.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: They're gathering everything they can before we shut it down.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: That's what it looks like. The tokens are still live right now.

threats.situation: Security detects a burst of activity across several compromised accounts: large cloud-file access, mailbox searches, unusual forwarding activity, and authentication tokens still in active use. The attacker may be preparing to leave with collected information.
evidence: Simultaneous large-volume file access across multiple compromised accounts
Mailbox search activity consistent with information gathering
New, unauthorized forwarding rules recently added
Authentication tokens for these accounts remain live right now

choices.label: Keep the sessions active briefly so Security can map the attacker's remaining access before beginning containment.
choices.consequence: The mapping proceeds, but every minute the tokens stay live is another minute of forwarding rules and file downloads completing successfully.

choices.label: Revoke suspicious sessions, block confirmed attacker infrastructure, and isolate affected accounts while preserving logs for investigation.
choices.consequence: The live tokens are cut immediately, stopping the exfiltration in progress, while the preserved logs still give investigators everything they need afterward.

choices.label: Block the known external infrastructure first and continue monitoring the active sessions to identify any additional compromised accounts.
choices.consequence: The blocked infrastructure slows the attacker down, but the still-active sessions keep pulling files and mail through channels that were never cut off.

threats.explanation: Once tokens are confirmed live during active exfiltration, every additional minute of observation has a real cost measured in data leaving the company. Logs preserved at the moment of containment provide the investigative value without extending a confirmed compromise.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: Yes. But it's connected to more than one account.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: Cloud storage. Mail. One endpoint. And at least one persistence mechanism.

opening.speaker: Mia
opening.text: So blocking another domain won't finish this.

opening.speaker: Mia
opening.text: Then we cut every path they have left.

ending.speaker: Mia
ending.text: Then why are we still seeing traffic?

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: Processes already in motion. Stop them before they reach the remaining systems.

resume_breach.speaker: Security Assistant
resume_breach.text: Containment is still running. Get the defenses back up.

breach_contained.speaker: Security Assistant
breach_contained.text: Breach contained. That path is cut, but more of their access is still live.

breach_contained.speaker: Mia
breach_contained.text: Then let's close the rest before they notice.

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: That's it. The phishing campaign is contained.

closing.speaker: Mia
closing.text: At the beginning, it was just one suspicious email.

closing.speaker: Security Assistant
closing.text: That's usually all an attacker needs.

closing.speaker: Mia
closing.text: And all we needed was to stop trusting the message and start verifying the situation.

threats.title: Active Session

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: The remaining suspicious cloud session is still authenticated.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Didn't the employee already change their password?

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: They did. The token never cared.

threats.situation: The remaining suspicious cloud session is still authenticated even though the employee's password has already been changed. The session token is still valid and has accessed several internal files. Terminating every session will force legitimate users to sign in again, but current logs are already preserved.
evidence: Employee's password was already changed
Session token for the suspicious session remains valid
The session has accessed several internal files
Current logs are already preserved and safe to act on

choices.label: Keep the session connected briefly while restricting file permissions so Security can observe whether it attempts to access another system.
choices.consequence: The permission restriction slows the session down, but it stays authenticated long enough to reach a second account before anyone acts further.

choices.label: Revoke all active sessions for the affected account, rotate its credentials, and require fresh authentication before restoring access.
choices.consequence: Every session tied to the account ends immediately. The employee re-authenticates cleanly and the account is fully contained.

choices.label: Revoke only the suspicious session and continue monitoring the employee's other authenticated sessions.
choices.consequence: The named session ends, but one of the employee's other 'legitimate' sessions turns out to be the attacker's actual foothold.

threats.explanation: A password change does not invalidate a session that was authenticated before it. Containment has to remove every potentially compromised authentication state, not only the one session that happened to be caught first.

threats.title: Hidden Forwarding Rule

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: After containing the session, I found an unusual mailbox rule.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: What does it do?

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Forwards selected messages to an external address, then marks them read. It's been there for days.

threats.situation: Security finds an unusual mailbox rule that automatically forwards selected messages to an external address and then marks them as read. The rule appears to have been created several days ago.
evidence: Forwarding rule sends selected messages to an external address
Rule marks forwarded messages as read, hiding them from the inbox view
Rule creation timestamp is several days old
No other persistence mechanisms have been confirmed yet

choices.label: Disable the rule without deleting it so investigators can preserve its configuration while watching for further attacker activity.
choices.consequence: The disabled rule stops forwarding, but leaving it intact means the attacker's fallback configuration is still sitting there, undiscovered persistence elsewhere included.

choices.label: Remove the rule, audit the mailbox for other persistence settings, review the external destination, and revoke remaining authorization tokens.
choices.consequence: The rule is gone and the audit turns up a second forwarding rule on a shared mailbox, which is removed before it does any damage.

choices.label: Remove the forwarding rule and monitor the mailbox closely for any new unauthorized configuration changes.
choices.consequence: The discovered rule is gone, but a second, unaudited rule on a shared mailbox keeps forwarding messages unnoticed.

threats.explanation: Finding one persistence mechanism does not prove it is the only one. A full audit of related mailboxes and authorization tokens is what actually closes the door, not just removing the rule that happened to be found first.

threats.title: Final Connection

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: One workstation is still talking to infrastructure tied to this campaign.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Whose is it?

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Someone currently working, with unsaved files open. This could be their last foothold.

threats.situation: Security correlates the remaining indicators to one workstation still communicating with infrastructure associated with the campaign. The endpoint belongs to an employee currently working, contains unsaved business data, has active network connections, and may contain the attacker's final foothold. Security already has sufficient centralized logs for initial investigation.
evidence: Workstation actively communicating with known campaign infrastructure
Employee is currently working with unsaved business data open
Endpoint has active network connections right now
Centralized logs already provide sufficient data for initial investigation

choices.label: Keep the endpoint connected under enhanced monitoring long enough to map any additional attacker infrastructure before isolating it.
choices.consequence: The mapping identifies more infrastructure, but the confirmed foothold stays online the entire time, continuing to communicate outward.

choices.label: Isolate the endpoint from the network, preserve its current state for forensics, and begin coordinated containment across linked accounts.
choices.consequence: The endpoint drops off the network immediately, its state preserved intact, while the linked accounts are contained in the same motion.

choices.label: Block the known malicious destinations at the network edge while keeping the workstation online so the employee can save and close active work.
choices.consequence: The known destinations are blocked, but the endpoint stays online and reachable long enough for the attacker to pivot through a channel that was never on the block list.

threats.explanation: Blocking known indicators only stops the traffic already identified. With enough evidence already gathered and a confirmed foothold still active, immediate isolation is what actually ends the exposure — extended observation at this point only extends the compromise.

opening.speaker: Leah
opening.text: Mia, can I ask you something?

opening.speaker: Leah
opening.text: Probably nothing. I keep getting weird texts.

opening.speaker: Leah
opening.text: That's the problem. I don't know.

opening.speaker: Leah
opening.text: I know what a scam looks like.
Mia brings the Security Assistant into the conversation.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: Let's see the messages before we decide what they are.

ending.speaker: Mia
ending.text: And when you opened the first message.

ending.speaker: Leah
ending.text: I was expecting this to be one stupid scam text.

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: It may have started with one text.

resume_breach.speaker: Security Assistant
resume_breach.text: Containment is still running. Get the defenses back up.

breach_contained.speaker: Security Assistant
breach_contained.text: Breach contained. That link is isolated, but Leah's other accounts still need checking.

breach_contained.speaker: Leah
breach_contained.text: Great. What's next?

threats.title: Mobile Account Warning

story.speaker: Leah
story.text: This is the first one. It says there's suspicious activity on my mobile account.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Does it look like it's really from your carrier?

story.speaker: Leah
story.text: The name looks right, but it's not anyone I have saved.

threats.situation: Leah receives an SMS saying suspicious activity was detected on her mobile account. The message contains Leah's real first and last name, her correct mobile carrier, the last four digits of her phone number, a case/reference number, and a link to "review activity." The sender name resembles her carrier but is not saved in her contacts.
evidence: Sender name resembles Leah's mobile carrier but is not a saved contact
Message includes Leah's real first and last name
Correct mobile carrier and the last four digits of her phone number
Includes a case/reference number and a link to "review activity"

choices.label: Open the link but avoid entering credentials unless the account information shown on the page matches Leah's actual details.
choices.consequence: Attacker-controlled pages may already know those details, so a matching page proves nothing. The page loads and begins harvesting information the moment it opens.

choices.label: Open the carrier's official app or manually visit the known carrier website/account portal and check account alerts there.
choices.consequence: The official app shows no such alert. The message is reported as fraud before Leah interacts with it further.

choices.label: Inspect the SMS link carefully and compare the domain with the carrier's normal website before deciding whether to open it.
choices.consequence: The domain looks close enough to pass a quick visual check, and opening it anyway still lands on a convincing lookalike page.

choices.label: Reply to the SMS asking the sender to provide the case number and more information before opening anything.
choices.consequence: The reply reaches the same untrusted channel, which happily supplies a convincing, fabricated case number right back.

threats.explanation: A sender name that resembles the carrier, and even accurate personal details, do not confirm the message actually came from the carrier. Verifying through a channel Leah already trusts — the official app or a manually typed address — is the only way to know if the alert is real.

threats.title: Transaction Alert

story.speaker: Leah
story.text: Another one. This time it says a transaction was attempted on my e-wallet.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Do you recognize the amount?

story.speaker: Leah
story.text: Honestly? It's small enough I might have just forgotten about it.

threats.situation: A second SMS claims a small transaction was attempted against Leah's e-wallet and offers a link: "Not you? Secure your account." The amount is believable and small enough that Leah isn't sure whether she simply forgot about it. She checks her phone and is still logged into her real e-wallet app.
evidence: Claimed transaction amount is small and plausible, so Leah isn't certain it's fake
SMS includes a "Not you? Secure your account." link
Leah's real e-wallet app is still logged in and reachable right now
No call has been made to any independently verified support line yet

choices.label: Use the SMS security link because Leah is still logged into the real app and can immediately change the password afterward if anything looks wrong.
choices.consequence: The link itself remains untrusted — being logged into the real app elsewhere doesn't make an attacker-controlled link safe, and opening it hands over the very session Leah was trying to protect.

choices.label: Open the real e-wallet app independently and review recent activity, security settings, and logged-in devices there.
choices.consequence: The real app shows no such transaction, confirming the SMS was fake. Leah reports it directly from an account she knows is genuine.

choices.label: Call the phone number printed in the SMS and ask support to verify whether the transaction exists.
choices.consequence: The printed number connects straight to the attacker's own call center, which happily "confirms" the fake transaction.

choices.label: Open the SMS link in a private/incognito browser only to compare the transaction details with the real app.
choices.consequence: Browser isolation does not establish legitimacy. The lookalike page still captures whatever Leah enters while making the comparison.

threats.explanation: Being logged into a real account elsewhere does not make an unrelated link safe, and a phone number or browser window supplied by the same suspicious message is still part of the untrusted channel. Verification has to start from an entry point Leah already knows independently.

threats.title: Support Follow-Up

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Leah?

story.speaker: Leah
story.text: What?

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: You're not telling me something.

story.speaker: Leah
story.text: ...It's nothing.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: You only say that when it isn't nothing.

story.speaker: Leah
story.text: I opened one of the messages earlier.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: You clicked it?

story.speaker: Leah
story.text: I didn't enter my password.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Which message?

story.speaker: Leah
story.text: The first one.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Why didn't you tell us?

story.speaker: Leah
story.text: Because I closed it. I thought that meant nothing happened.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Maybe nothing did. But now we treat that interaction as evidence.
Shortly after, another text arrives claiming to be from mobile support.

story.speaker: Leah
story.text: How do they know I opened it?

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: That's what I want to know.

threats.situation: A new SMS claims to be from mobile support: "We detected that you opened a suspicious verification page. Your account has been temporarily protected. Complete the security review below." It is alarming because it appears to know Leah interacted with the earlier link. It includes the correct carrier, Leah's name, the approximate time of her earlier interaction, and a new security-case number.
evidence: Message references the approximate time Leah opened the earlier SMS link
Uses the correct carrier name and Leah's real name
Provides a new security-case number, different from the first message's
No verified carrier system has ever contacted Leah about this before now

choices.label: Follow the security-review link because the sender accurately knows about Leah's earlier interaction, then stop if it requests sensitive information.
choices.consequence: Knowledge of an event does not prove identity. The page begins harvesting information the moment it opens, well before Leah gets the chance to decide to stop.

choices.label: Use a separately obtained carrier support channel or official app to verify whether any security case actually exists and review account access.
choices.consequence: The verified channel confirms no such case was ever opened, and Leah's account is checked clean through a source she actually trusts.

choices.label: Compare the new case number with the reference number from the first SMS and continue only if the records appear consistent.
choices.consequence: Both numbers came from the same attacker, so of course they line up. Leah continues straight into the fake review.

choices.label: Ask the sender to explain what activity triggered the warning without opening the new link.
choices.consequence: Still interacting with the attacker-controlled channel, and replying only confirms the number is active and being watched.

threats.explanation: Knowing that Leah opened an earlier message only proves the attacker was watching that first interaction — it says nothing about who they actually are. Real verification has to come from a channel Leah reached on her own, never from the same thread that already proved it can't be trusted.

opening.speaker: Leah
opening.text: The headphones I ordered three days ago.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: Are you actually expecting them today?

opening.speaker: Leah
opening.text: This is what I don't understand.

opening.speaker: Leah
opening.text: How would a scammer know what I'm waiting for?

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: That's what we're going to find out.

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: The messages followed the real delivery almost in real time.

ending.speaker: Leah
ending.text: So somebody has access to my shopping account?

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: We need to identify what information they actually have.

The real Mia is messaging Leah right now through the already-known number

choices.consequence: The sender answers convincingly, likely drawing on Leah and Mia's own social media or past conversations, and the improvised test passes.

choices.label: Save the new number temporarily but keep the old number until Mia confirms.

threats.explanation: A familiar nickname and accurate personal context prove the attacker has studied this relationship, not that the message came from Mia. Verification has to happen through the channel already known to be hers, never the new one presenting itself.

Names the café Mia normally visits
Requested amount (₱1,200) is a believable, unremarkable sum
Casual phrasing matches Mia's normal texting style
The real Mia is sitting next to Leah right now, not stuck anywhere

choices.label: Confirm the request through the known Mia contact or voice/video channel before sending money.
choices.consequence: Reaching the real Mia directly confirms she never sent the request, and no money goes to the impersonating number.

choices.consequence: The sender supplies another convincing detail drawn from the same research, and the transfer proceeds on confidence that was never actually earned.

threats.explanation: Matching someone's real schedule and speaking style shows the attacker has studied the relationship, not that they are the person being impersonated. Only a channel independently known to reach the real Mia can confirm a request like this.

evidence: Knows Leah's cousin's name
Knows her mother's first name
References the hospital/clinic the family normally uses
References a recent family event
Explicitly asks Leah not to call her mother to confirm

threats.situation: Leah receives several legitimate OTPs from a service she actually uses, arriving in the same sender thread where genuine codes have appeared before. She is still able to access the account normally, and there is currently no visible unauthorized transaction.
evidence: Messages come from the same legitimate sender thread as past genuine codes
Multiple OTPs arrived without Leah requesting any of them
Leah can still log into the account normally right now
No unauthorized transaction or change is currently visible

choices.label: Use the security link from a follow-up SMS to review the attempted login, since the OTP itself came through the account's legitimate message thread.
choices.consequence: A legitimate OTP thread doesn't make a separate follow-up link legitimate. The link leads to a lookalike page built to harvest the very credentials Leah is trying to protect.

choices.label: Open the service independently, review recent sign-in activity and security settings, and secure the account if an unfamiliar authentication attempt appears.
choices.consequence: The independent review turns up an unfamiliar sign-in attempt from an unrecognized device, which is closed before it goes any further.

choices.label: Change the account password immediately but leave existing sessions and recovery settings unchanged.
choices.consequence: The new password blocks new attempts, but a session or recovery method already in motion is left completely untouched by a password change alone.

choices.label: Wait for the OTP attempts to stop because whoever is trying to sign in cannot finish authentication without the code.
choices.consequence: The attempts eventually stop, but not because the danger passed. Whoever was behind them simply moved to a different entry point that doesn't need this OTP at all.

threats.explanation: Holding onto the OTP prevented this one attempt, but repeated authentication requests are themselves evidence that something needs to be investigated and secured, not simply outlasted or resolved by a password change alone.

threats.title: Cancel the Request

story.speaker: Leah
story.text: The e-wallet just sent a real code. But now a different number is texting: 'We detected an unauthorized account recovery request. To CANCEL this request, verify the six-digit code that was just sent to your registered number.'

story.speaker: Leah
story.text: Wait. They want the code to cancel it?

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: That's backwards, right?

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Think about who generated the code.

threats.situation: A legitimate OTP arrives from Leah's e-wallet. Seconds later, a different number sends: "We detected an unauthorized account recovery request. To CANCEL this request, verify the six-digit code that was just sent to your registered number." The message doesn't claim the code will authorize access — it claims providing it will cancel the attack.
evidence: Legitimate OTP arrived from the e-wallet's own verified sender
A second, different number claims a recovery request must be "cancelled"
The cancellation message asks Leah to verify the code that was just sent to her
No genuine fraud-prevention process asks a customer to supply their own OTP

choices.label: Provide the OTP because the message says it will CANCEL rather than approve the recovery request.
choices.consequence: The wording is reversed, not the outcome. Whoever generated the recovery request now has the exact code needed to complete it.

choices.label: Ignore the follow-up instructions and independently open/contact the e-wallet through its known app or support channel to investigate the recovery attempt.
choices.consequence: The e-wallet's own support confirms the recovery attempt and cancels it directly, with no code ever leaving Leah's phone.

choices.label: Call the support number included in the cancellation message and ask them to verify the recovery request before discussing the code.
choices.consequence: The number belongs to the same attacker, who happily "confirms" their own fabricated case.

choices.label: Reply that Leah did not request the recovery, but refuse to provide the OTP unless the sender proves the case is legitimate.
choices.consequence: No code is given, but replying confirms the number is active and keeps the conversation going through the same untrusted channel.

threats.explanation: Whoever generated the request is the only one who benefits from the code, no matter which direction the message claims it moves the process. A wallet provider's real fraud team never needs the customer to supply a code that was sent to stop something.

threats.situation: Leah receives a legitimate notification from her primary email provider: "A password reset was requested." evidence: Legitimate "password reset requested" notification from the real provider
An unfamiliar device recently appeared in account activity
Leah remains signed in on her own phone right now
A follow-up SMS claims to be the provider's "Account Protection Team" and asks Leah to avoid changing her password or security settings

choices.consequence: Acting through the still-active session cuts off the unfamiliar device immediately and confirms the recovery methods haven't already been altered.

choices.label: Change the password immediately through the real provider, but postpone reviewing sessions and recovery methods until the reset attempts stop.
choices.consequence: The new password stops new attempts, but the unfamiliar device's existing session and any already-changed recovery method are left completely untouched.

choices.label: Keep the current password temporarily and monitor the unfamiliar device while independently contacting the provider's real support channel.
choices.consequence: The verification itself is genuine, but the unfamiliar device stays authenticated and able to act the entire time contact and confirmation are pending.

threats.explanation: A real account-protection team never asks the account owner to leave a suspicious session running. The urgency to "not interfere" is what keeps the actual foothold — the authenticated session — alive the longest.

One unfamiliar device is still trusted on the account
Leah retains access to one previously authenticated device right now
An unfamiliar number is offering "emergency" restoration by SMS reply

choices.consequence: The trusted device carries enough standing access to reach the real recovery workflow, and the review finds the unfamiliar device still holding a live session — it's revoked immediately.

I'll return it tonight." The messages sound like Leah, and at least one relative has already replied.

The wording and tone convincingly sound like Leah
At least one relative has already replied to the compromised account
Warning contacts from the same compromised account would use the attacker's own channel
